record.original_question: Let G be a locally-finite simple geodetic graph and let t be a natural number. If C is an embedded cycle whose diameter exceeds t and whose length is minimal among all such paths in G, must C contain a geodesic subpath of length t + 1?

evidence.quote: It is known that the general classification problem of geodetic graphs is related to the problem of the study of rewriting systems, which, at the same time, connects abstract algebra and theoretical computer science [2, 3]. As a result, a new contribution to a better understanding of the description of geodetic graphs consists in proving several conjectures, among them, the following one:

Let G be a locally-finite simple geodetic graph, and t ∈ N. If C is an embedded cycle of diameter exceeding t that has minimal length among all such paths in G, then C contains a geodesic subpath of length t + 1.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
A simple graph $G$ is called geodetic if between any two vertices of $G$ there is a unique shortest path. The graph $G$ is locally finite if every vertex has finite degree. A cycle $C$ in $G$ is called embedded if it is an induced subgraph (no chords). The diameter of $C$ is the maximum distance, taken in $G$, between two vertices of $C$. A geodesic subpath of $G$ of length $\ell$ is a path with $\ell$ edges that is a shortest path between its endpoints in $G$.

Let $G$ be a locally-finite simple geodetic graph and let $t \in \mathbb{N}$. Suppose $C$ is an embedded cycle of $G$ whose diameter in $G$ exceeds $t$, and which has minimal length among all embedded cycles of $G$ with diameter exceeding $t$. Prove or disprove: $C$ must contain a geodesic subpath of length $t+1$.
artifact.status_search_result: The full classification of geodetic graphs remains open more than sixty years after Ore posed it. The conjecture about embedded cycles of minimal length containing a geodesic subpath of length t+1 is stated as a conjecture and recent (2026) work on geodetic graphs via embedded even graphs investigates related structural questions but does not appear to resolve this specific conjecture.
